title: Artificial Intelligence: Council and Parliament agree to simplify and streamline rules
date_evidence: On 7 May 2026, negotiators from the Council of the European Union, the European Parliament, and the European Commission reached a provisional agreement on the terms of the Digital Omnibus on AI
key_claim: On 7 May 2026 the Council and Parliament agreed a Digital Omnibus deal deferring the AI Act's high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I) and pushing transparency duties to 2 December 2026.
frame_summary: Argues the EU is amending and deferring its own AI Act for the first time since adoption to simplify the rulebook and buy industry time, in the name of competitiveness.
signals_supported: EU AI Act deferral and simplification

title: Council signs off simplification of sustainability reporting and due diligence requirements to boost EU competitiveness
date_evidence: On 24 February 2026, the EU formally adopted the Omnibus I package, a wide-ranging simplification initiative that amends the CSRD and CSDDD
key_claim: On 24 February 2026 the Council signed off the Omnibus I package narrowing CSRD and CSDDD scope, raising CSRD thresholds to more than 1,000 employees and above EUR 450 million turnover and CSDDD to more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5 billion.
frame_summary: Argues the EU is deliberately rolling back the scope of its flagship sustainability reporting and due-diligence rules to cut compliance burden and restore competitiveness.
verbatim_quote: raising its thresholds to companies with more than 1,000 employees and above EUR 450 million net annual turnover; the CS3D scope is narrowed by raising its thresholds to companies with more than 5,000 employees and above EUR 1.5 billion net turnover

title: Digital Omnibus: EDPB and EDPS support simplification and competitiveness while raising key concerns
date_evidence: Digital Omnibus: EDPB and EDPS support simplification and competitiveness while raising key concerns 11 February 2026 ... Brussels, 11 February
key_claim: The EDPB and EDPS support the Digital Omnibus simplification aim but strongly urge co-legislators not to adopt the proposed change to the GDPR definition of personal data, which would significantly narrow the concept of personal data.
frame_summary: Argues simplification is welcome for competitiveness but warns that the proposed redefinition of personal data goes beyond the GDPR and CJEU case law and would weaken protection of individual rights.
signals_supported: EU data-protection and digital-rules simplification (Digital Omnibus)

title: Omnibus numerique : le CEPD et l'EDPS soutiennent la simplification et la competitivite tout en soulevant des preoccupations majeures
date_evidence: On February 11, 2026, the CEPD and EDPS published a joint opinion confirming the relevance of concerns about these proposals and requesting notably the rejection of certain key modifications to the RGPD
key_claim: The CNIL relays that the EDPB and EDPS joint opinion recognises the Digital Omnibus simplification aim but rejects or criticises several proposals, notably the redefinition of personal data at the heart of the GDPR.
frame_summary: Argues, from the French regulator's vantage, that the digital-rules simplification drive is legitimate on competitiveness grounds but several proposals risk lowering data-protection guarantees.
signals_supported: EU data-protection and digital-rules simplification (Digital Omnibus)

title: Europe Tech Regulation: Yes to Simplification, No to Deregulation
date_evidence: Published date: February 10, 2026 ... Europe Tech Regulation: Yes to Simplification, No to Deregulation
key_claim: Europe is course-correcting on tech rules under a competitiveness banner, with von der Leyen's watchwords now competitiveness, growth and simplification, but the word deregulate remains taboo in the proposals.
frame_summary: Argues the EU is simplifying rather than deregulating: the political framing is competitiveness-driven walk-back of compliance burden, not abandonment of the underlying regulatory aims.
signals_supported: EU AI Act deferral and simplification

title: EU Omnibus I Directive amending CSRD and CSDDD enters into force
date_evidence: EU Omnibus I Directive amending CSRD and CSDDD will enter into force on 18 March 2026
key_claim: The Omnibus I amending Directive entered into force on 18 March 2026; Member States must transpose the CSRD changes by 19 March 2027 and CSDDD by 26 July 2028, with wave-3 listed SMEs removed from CSRD scope.
frame_summary: Argues the sustainability-rules rollback is now operative law, not a proposal: the amending Directive is in force and member states are on a transposition clock.

title: Treasury Proposes Rule to Implement the GENIUS Act's Requirements to Counter Illicit Finance
date_evidence: Treasury Proposes Rule to Implement the GENIUS Act's Requirements to Counter Illicit Finance April 8, 2026 WASHINGTON
key_claim: On 8 April 2026 FinCEN and OFAC issued a joint proposed rule implementing the GENIUS Act's anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations for permitted payment stablecoin issuers, treating them as Bank Secrecy Act financial institutions.
frame_summary: Argues the US is rapidly building a federal payment-stablecoin rulebook under the GENIUS Act, asserting national leadership over digital-asset rules through fast agency rulemaking.
signals_supported: US GENIUS Act stablecoin rulemaking build-out
cluster: Multilateral rulebooks splinter into national tracks

title: OCC Proposes Regulations to Implement GENIUS Act
date_evidence: sullcrom.com/insights/memo/2026/March/OCC-Proposes-Regulations-Implement-GENIUS-Act: on February 25, 2026 the OCC issued a notice of proposed rulemaking to implement provisions of the GENIUS Act
key_claim: The OCC issued its GENIUS Act notice of proposed rulemaking on 25 February 2026, with the statute's implementing regulations due by 18 July 2026.
frame_summary: Argues the US federal stablecoin regime is being stood up at speed across multiple agencies, evidencing a national rulebook taking shape on a statutory clock.

title: Global Anti-Base Erosion Model Rules (Pillar Two), Side-by-Side Package
date_evidence: The OECD released a side-by-side package on January 5, 2026, to address U.S. concerns about the global minimum tax (Pillar Two)
key_claim: On 5 January 2026 the OECD published a side-by-side package implementing the G7's June 2025 deal to exclude US-parented groups from the global minimum tax's income inclusion and undertaxed profits rules; the US is so far the only jurisdiction the OECD recognises as qualifying.
frame_summary: Argues the OECD has accommodated US demands by carving US multinationals out of the global minimum tax, signalling that the multilateral tax consensus now bends to national leverage.
signals_supported: OECD Pillar Two US side-by-side carve-out
cluster: Multilateral rulebooks splinter into national tracks

title: International Tax Policy: Where the U.S. Stands and What's Ahead in 2026
date_evidence: International Tax Policy: Where the U.S. Stands and What's Ahead in 2026 ... Date: January 7, 2026
key_claim: Most of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's international tax changes take effect from 1 January 2026, and the US side-by-side arrangement reshapes how US multinationals sit relative to the OECD global minimum tax.
frame_summary: Argues US international tax policy in 2026 is on a distinct national track that diverges from, and now partly overrides, the multilateral OECD settlement.
signals_supported: OECD Pillar Two US side-by-side carve-out

title: Examining the Landscape and Limitations of the Federal Push to Override State AI Regulation
date_evidence: ropesgray.com/en/insights/alerts/2026/03/examining-the-landscape-and-limitations-of-the-federal-push-to-override-state-ai-regulation: the 11 December 2025 executive order directs an AI Litigation Task Force and agency reviews by 11 March 2026
key_claim: The 11 December 2025 executive order seeks a national AI policy that would override state AI laws via a Litigation Task Force and agency reviews due 11 March 2026, though preemption by executive order alone is legally limited and state laws remain in effect.
frame_summary: Argues Washington is trying to impose a single national AI standard over a patchwork of state laws, but that the executive route is legally constrained, so the federal-versus-state contest is unresolved.
cluster: Multilateral rulebooks splinter into national tracks

title: FCA sets out next phase of smarter, more effective regulation
date_evidence: FCA sets out next phase of smarter, more effective regulation (Story date: March 26, 2026)
key_claim: The FCA's 2026/27 work programme sets out a smarter, more data-driven regulator using AI to speed authorisations, and reiterates it does not plan AI-specific rules, overseeing AI through existing regimes.
frame_summary: Argues the UK is deliberately not building bespoke AI rules, instead leaning on existing supervisory regimes and a pro-growth simplification of its own regulator, a third national posture distinct from the EU and US.
cluster: Multilateral rulebooks splinter into national tracks

title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Information technology - Artificial intelligence - Management system
date_evidence: meta-pubdate: 20231218; General information Status: Published Publication date: 2023-12; standing standard reference page, accessed 19/06/2026
key_claim: ISO/IEC 42001 is the world's first AI management system standard, specifying requirements for an AI management system and increasingly adopted by vendors as a voluntary certification baseline.
frame_summary: Argues a voluntary international management standard exists and is positioned as the cross-border baseline for responsible AI governance independent of any single jurisdiction's statute.
cluster: Voluntary standards become the working baseline

title: Where does the world stand on ISSB adoption?
date_evidence: May 2026 - Where does the world stand on ISSB adoption? | S&P Global
key_claim: As of 22 April 2026, 28 jurisdictions have adopted the ISSB sustainability disclosure standards on a voluntary or mandatory basis, with a further 12 planning to do so, including UK and South Korea standards built on the ISSB baseline.
frame_summary: Argues the ISSB sustainability-disclosure standards are consolidating into a global baseline adopted jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction, even as the EU narrows its own statutory reporting scope.
cluster: Voluntary standards become the working baseline
